act3b.old: The customers paid first. Unauthorized accounts generated unauthorized fees. Overdraft charges for accounts they didn't know existed. Annual fees for credit cards they never applied for. Hits to their credit scores when those cards went unpaid. Some customers were denied mortgages because of the damage to their credit. Others couldn't get car loans. A few lost their homes. The bank collected an estimated 2.6 million dollars in fees from accounts customers never authorized. That's the official number. The real number is almost certainly higher. Meanwhile, between 2011 and 2016, Wells Fargo said it fired more than 5,300 employees for sales-practice violations. Some had opened unauthorized accounts. Others said they had been punished for resisting impossible quotas or reporting misconduct. Different conduct. Same institution. The people who missed their targets were pushed out. The people who cheated to meet them could be fired. And some of the people who warned the bank said they were fired too.

act4.old: The Los Angeles Times broke the story in 2013. Reporter E. Scott Reckard documented the pressure, the unauthorized accounts and the firings. The city of Los Angeles sued. Federal regulators followed. In 2016, Wells Fargo agreed to pay 185 million dollars in penalties. John Stumpf went before Congress that September. Senator Elizabeth Warren asked whether he had returned any of his compensation. At that point, he had not. He retired the next month. Wells Fargo's board later clawed back or cancelled roughly 69 million dollars of his compensation. Carrie Tolstedt, who ran the Community Bank, had retired with holdings initially valued near 125 million dollars. The board later clawed back or forfeited roughly 67 million dollars from her and said she would receive no severance. But the story kept widening. The estimate of potentially unauthorized accounts rose from about 2 million to 3.5 million. Separate investigations found hundreds of thousands of customers charged for unwanted auto insurance, with some borrowers losing their vehicles, as well as improper mortgage fees and failures across other product lines. In 2018, the Federal Reserve capped Wells Fargo's growth until the bank fixed its governance and risk controls. The Fed removed that cap in June 2025, then terminated the remaining 2018 enforcement action in March 2026. By then, the cost was far beyond 3 billion dollars. A single 2022 consumer-protection order required 3.7 billion dollars in penalties and customer redress.
